extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecution practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including how to identify abstract ideas/mental processes, laws of nature/natural phenomena/products of nature, and how to apply the markedly different characteristics analysis and tentative abstract idea procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can recite a mental process even if they are claimed as being performed on a computer. A claimed step that can be performed mentally (e.g., with pen and paper) qualifies as a mental process and thus can be an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look to the specification and case law (e.g., CyberSource; Flook; Univ. of Florida Research Foundation; Symantec) when determining whether claimed steps are mental processes. If steps can be performed mentally or with pen and paper, treat the limitation as a mental process (abstract idea). Examples given include listings of credit card transactions, computations that "can be made by pencil and paper calculations," and data analysis described as performed with "pen and paper methodologies".

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate computer-implemented claims using the specification and BRI for mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating whether a claim that requires a computer recites a mental process, examiners should carefully consider the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the specification to determine if the claimed invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and applicant is merely claiming that concept performed (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. In such situations the claim is considered to recite a mental process. Case examples include Benson and Mortgage Grader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps merely perform a mental concept on a generic computer, the claim can be directed to an abstract idea despite requiring a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting votes are "human cognitive actions" even when performed on a computer) and Versata (determining a price using general-purpose hardware was described as the abstract idea of determining a price). Treat claims that merely map a mental concept onto generic computing hardware as directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed computer-implemented steps mirror human cognitive actions in a computer environment, the claims can be directed to a mental process (abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Symantec (electronic post office steps analogous to deciding whether to read or dispose of mail) and FairWarning (analyzing access logs by rules that mirror human questions for detecting fraud). If, aside from generic computer steps, nothing in the claims forecloses human performance, treat as a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that use a computer only as a tool to perform a concept humans could perform without a computer can be directed to a mental process (abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping concept implemented using databases and grading modules) and Berkheimer (parsing and evaluating data at a high level of generality using a computer). High-level recitation of data manipulation that merely uses computers as tools supports a finding of an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and process claims can both recite mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Both product claims (e.g., computer systems, computer-readable media) and process claims may recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not assume that only method claims recite mental processes. Examples include a computer-implemented system and method claiming anonymous loan shopping (Mortgage Grader), systems for detecting improper access (FairWarning), and inputting information from hard copy into a program (Content Extraction & Transmission). The term "mental processes" refers to a type of abstract idea, not the statutory category of claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract idea procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A "tentative abstract idea" is a claim limitation the examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tentative abstract ideas under the subject matter eligibility framework: - If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A; NO) → eligible at Pathway B (analysis concludes). - If the claim does not integrate the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) → requires Step 2B analysis: if the claim provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) → eligible at Pathway C. - If the claim does not provide an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO) → bring to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) director; a rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director and the approval recorded in the file.

rubrics_metrics.name: TC Director approval and procedure for tentative abstract idea rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A Step 2B subject matter eligibility rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea requires TC Director approval and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should identify that the claim(s) are directed to a previously non-enumerated abstract idea via form paragraph 7.05.017 and include the TC Director’s signature. The TC Director will inform Patents Management so the public can be notified. An interview with the examiner may be conducted after a Step 2B rejection, and an interview with the approving TC Director is not necessary for applications where the TC Director approval was used. The examiner retains authority to withdraw or maintain the rejection upon consideration of applicant’s reply and is not required to obtain TC Director approval to withdraw or maintain such a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or do not have markedly different characteristics from what occurs in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have described these exceptions using terms like "physical phenomena," "scientific principles," and "products of nature." Examples cited: isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned farm animal (Roslin), correlations between genetic regions (Genetic Techs. v. Merial), metabolic correlations (Mayo), presence of biomarkers (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health), electromagnetism (O’Reilly v. Morse), qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry Genetics), chemical principles (Tilghman), cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), genotype/medication relationships (Vanda). These exceptions reflect that basic scientific tools are not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not every claim mentioning natural abilities is a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim describing a natural ability, quality, or process does not automatically recite a law of nature or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claims reciting process steps for fractionating, recovering, and cryopreserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect) were eligible because they were not focused on merely observing or detecting an ability. Similarly, a method of treating cancer with chemotherapy or treating headaches with aspirin is not considered a law of nature when focused on the treatment steps. Such claims are eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception, in which case further analysis (Prong Two/Step 2B) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature and broadly reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Product of nature exceptions include both naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts; BRI can encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Myriad (isolated DNA) and Ambry Genetics (primers) were treated as products of nature. A synthetic product structurally identical to a natural counterpart remains a product of nature. Under BRI, a claim to a nature-based product (e.g., "cloned giraffe") may encompass embodiments with and without markedly different characteristics. If a claim recites a product of nature and is rejected for lacking an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), examiners should point out the BRI and recommend narrowing amendments where possible to focus on embodiments that are not products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (purpose and outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to determine whether a nature-based product limitation is a "product of nature" exception (part of Step 2A Prong One).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: - If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present. - If the claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., "a Lactobacillus bacterium") and markedly different characteristics are shown, no further eligibility analysis is necessary (Step 2B not required). - If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, then the claim recites a product of nature and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and potentially Step 2B). Case law: Chakrabarty (bacterium with markedly different characteristics not a product of nature) and Roslin (cloned sheep lacked markedly different characteristics and was a product of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim, and avoid over-extending the analysis to claim elements that are not nature-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product of nature exception. The analysis should be limited to the nature-based product limitations to determine whether they are product of nature exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-based products (living organisms, synthetic products) require markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-naturally occurring products (including living organisms and synthetic products) are not automatically eligible simply because they were created by human ingenuity; eligibility depends on whether they possess markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roslin (cloned sheep treated as product of nature); Chakrabarty (bacterium with markedly different characteristics eligible). Examiners should evaluate whether the claimed nature-based product possesses markedly different characteristics; if not, treat as product of nature and continue eligibility analysis. For claims that nevertheless are directed to inventions that clearly do not tie up a judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis of MPEP § 2106.06 is appropriate.
